title: B2+ · L4 — Technical interviews
description: Pensar en voz alta durante entrevistas tecnicas: explicar razonamiento, admitir incertidumbre elegantemente, hacer preguntas clarificadoras.

questions.prompt: Coding interview en vivo con un ingeniero de Google. Comparte contigo un problema en HackerRank.
questions.question: You're given a coding problem. Which is the BEST opener to think aloud?
options: Let me talk through my thinking before I write any code.
questions.explanation: 'Let me talk through my thinking' es la apertura estandar en tech interviews FAANG. Los entrevistadores VALORAN el proceso mas que la solucion final — con codigo perfecto pero sin explicacion se suele rechazar. Codear en silencio es error CRITICO de novato: el interviewer no puede evaluar como razonas ni intervenir con hints. 'I know this' delata arrogancia. Colocacion nativa: 'talk through' (explicar paso a paso) vs 'talk about' (mencionar).
examples: Before I start coding, let me talk through my approach so you can catch any wrong assumptions early. → apertura pulida
Let me walk you through my thinking — happy to be interrupted if I'm going off track. → invita colaboracion

questions.prompt: El interviewer describe un problema y no te da todos los detalles.
questions.question: You need to ask a clarifying question. Which is most natural?
options: Just to clarify — are we assuming the input is always sorted?
questions.explanation: 'Just to clarify — [pregunta especifica sobre assumption]' es la formula tipo. Preguntar sobre input, edge cases, tamano y constraints ANTES de codear es SENAL DE SENIORIDAD — los junior asumen y fallan; los senior verifican. Error hispano: 'Explain me' — en ingles falta el 'to' obligatorio ('explain TO me') y ademas suena a orden. 'What?' es grosero. Colocacion nativa: 'Just to clarify' vs 'Just to confirm' (esta segunda cuando ya intuyes la respuesta y quieres validar).
examples: Just to clarify — can the input contain duplicates, or are elements guaranteed to be unique?
Quick clarifying question: what's the expected size of the input? Are we talking hundreds, or millions?

questions.statement: It's better to stay silent while thinking hard, so the interviewer sees you concentrating.
questions.explanation: FALSO — es el error #1 en tech interviews. El silencio prolongado (>10 segundos) es una senal roja: el interviewer no puede evaluar tu razonamiento ni ayudarte. La regla es simple: 'if you're thinking, you're talking'. Cultura clave: en anglo se valora explicitar todo, incluso las dudas ('I'm not sure if...', 'I'm considering two approaches...'). El silencio en cambio se interpreta como 'no sabe' o 'esta perdido'. Hispanohablantes suelen callar por respeto — aqui es contraproducente.
examples: Weak: [30 seconds of silence while staring at screen] → red flag
Strong: I'm thinking a hash map might work here — let me sketch it out and see if the complexity checks out. → transparencia total

questions.prompt: Llevas 8 minutos con un algoritmo y no ves la solucion. Necesitas admitirlo sin parecer perdido.
questions.question: You're stuck. Which is the best way to admit it professionally?
options: I'm blanking — mind if I take a step back and think about it differently?
questions.explanation: 'I'm blanking' + 'take a step back' es la formula ideal: honesto sin ser derrotista, y activa la posibilidad de un hint. 'I'm blanking' = se me esta yendo, colocacion nativa (literalmente 'estar en blanco'). 'Take a step back' es la metafora estandar para replantear. Error hispano: 'this is impossible' — dramatico y arrogante (implicas que la pregunta es mala). Los interviewers valoran mucho la respuesta al bloqueo — es literalmente una de las senales evaluadas.
examples: I'm blanking on the exact syntax — mind if I pseudocode it first and clean it up later? → pide flexibilidad
Let me take a step back and reconsider the problem from scratch — I think I've been overcomplicating it. → self-diagnosis

questions.text: The brute force approach would work but it's quadratic — let me see if I can do better with a hash map.
questions.explanation: Frase absolutamente clasica en coding interviews. Fenomeno de connected speech: 'it's quadratic' con /tskw/ tri-cluster consonantico dificil, tiende a elidir la /t/ dejando /ɪskwɒˈdrætɪk/. 'Would work' con weak form /wədwɜːk/. Vocabulario tecnico esencial: 'brute force' (fuerza bruta / solucion naive), 'quadratic' (O(n²)), 'hash map' (estructura de datos). Muestra pensamiento en complejidad computacional — obligatorio en senior interviews.
examples: The naive solution is O(n squared) — can we do better with sorting first?
Brute force works, but let me try to optimize with a two-pointer approach instead.

questions.prompt: El interviewer te pregunta la complejidad de un algoritmo y no estas 100% seguro.
questions.question: Which is the most professional way to hedge when uncertain about a technical detail?
options: I might be wrong on this — I believe it's O(log n), but I'd double-check.
questions.explanation: Triple formula magica: humildad ('I might be wrong') + commitment con hipotesis ('I believe X') + rigor ('but I'd double-check'). Suena muy senior porque combina confianza (te mojas) con honestidad (admites incertidumbre) sin colapsar en 'no se'. 'Maybe' es demasiado tibio; 'I forgot' es fatal (implica que sabias y olvidaste, no que no dominas). Registro clave: los senior engineers SIEMPRE hedge cuando no estan seguros — es senal de experiencia, no de debilidad.
examples: I'm about 80% sure this is O(n log n), but I'd verify with the docs before shipping. → probabilidad numerica
My gut says use a queue here, but let me reason through it out loud to check. → hedge + think aloud

questions.prompt: Empareja cada frase tecnica idiomatica con su traduccion:

pairs.left: Let me walk you through the trade-offs.
pairs.right: Dejame explicarte los pros y contras.

pairs.left: I'll come back to that edge case.

questions.explanation: Cinco frases de vocabulario tecnico indispensables en entrevistas de ingenieria. 'Walk through trade-offs' (analizar pros y contras); 'edge case' (caso limite, singular y sin articulo indefinido en spoken tech); 'scales linearly' (crecimiento lineal — muy distinto de 'grows in a line' que seria calco); 'subtle bug' (colocacion nativa, no 'small bug'); 'refactor' (verbo tecnico anglizado incluso en espanol). Todos son universalmente reconocidos en cualquier tech interview.
examples: Let me walk you through the trade-offs between the two designs before we pick one.
I want to come back to that edge case once the main path works — remind me if I forget.

questions.target: Before I dive in, I want to confirm the constraints — what's the expected input size, and are we optimizing for time or space?
questions.explanation: Apertura senior perfecta para cualquier system design o coding interview. 'Dive in' (phrasal verb para 'ponerse manos a la obra'); 'constraints' (restricciones tecnicas — obligatorio pregunta); 'optimizing for time or space' es la dicotomia clasica de algoritmos. Preguntar ANTES = mindset de arquitecto senior. Ritmo natural: pausa breve tras 'constraints —' (guion largo marca pausa reflexiva). Contracciones: 'what's', 'we're' obligatorias — 'what is', 'we are' completos suenan a lectura de guion.
examples: Quick question before I start — what are we optimizing for, latency or throughput?
Just to set expectations — how large can the input get, and what's the acceptable response time?

questions.prompt: Terminaste de escribir codigo. El interviewer te pide trazar la ejecucion con un input de ejemplo.
questions.question: You've written buggy code. The interviewer asks you to trace through an example. What's best?
options: Let me trace through this with the example — I'll walk you through step by step.
questions.explanation: 'Trace through step by step' es la respuesta correcta y ademas te ayuda a ENCONTRAR bugs solo (muy comun). Los interviewers piden trace precisamente para ver si detectas tus propios errores. 'It should work' y 'trust me' son el sello del junior arrogante — red flag inmediato. Colocacion nativa: 'trace through' (recorrer la ejecucion) vs 'dry-run' (ejecutar en papel) — ambas validas. Registro: 'walk you through' es la formula de referencia.
examples: Let me trace through this carefully with the sample input to make sure the logic holds. → rigor
I'll dry-run this on a small example first — always catches bugs I missed. → auto-critico maduro

questions.statement: Asking about edge cases (empty input, duplicates, negative numbers) shows weakness.
questions.explanation: FALSO. Pensar en edge cases es LA senal #1 de senioridad en tech interviews. Los junior escriben la solucion happy-path y fallan; los senior enumeran edge cases ANTES de codear: null, empty, duplicates, negatives, overflow, unicode, off-by-one. Muchas empresas (Amazon, Google) tienen edge-case-handling como criterio explicito de evaluacion. Registro: usa 'handle' + edge case ('how do we handle empty input?') como colocacion fija.
examples: What should happen if the input is empty? Do we return null, throw, or return an empty result?
Do we need to handle Unicode characters, or can we assume ASCII only? → aclara alcance

questions.prompt: Llevas 5 minutos atascado y el interviewer te sugiere una pista.
questions.question: The interviewer suggests a hint. Which is the best response?
options: That's a great pointer — let me try that direction.
questions.explanation: Reconocer el hint con gratitud + aplicarlo activamente es la respuesta ideal — muestra teachability, un rasgo altisimamente valorado (Google llama a esto 'general cognitive ability + learn'). 'I don't need help' es red flag masiva: sugiere ego mayor que la propia capacidad. 'Whatever' u 'okay' secos suenan a indiferencia. Colocacion nativa: 'great pointer' o 'helpful nudge' (nudge = empujoncito, muy usado en tech culture US) son formas elegantes de agradecer sin adular.
examples: Ah, that's a helpful nudge — let me think about it that way. → agradecimiento breve pero real
Good catch — I hadn't considered that angle. Let me redo the analysis from there. → nombra que aporta

questions.text: I'd argue this design scales better long-term, though it does add some upfront complexity.
questions.explanation: Frase clasica de system design senior. Fenomeno de connected speech: 'I'd argue' con weak form /aɪdˈɑːɡjuː/; 'does add' con enfasis contrastivo en 'does' (emphatic do — muy nativo). 'Long-term' pronunciado como una unidad /lɒŋtɜːm/. Colocaciones: 'scales better' (colocacion nativa para escalabilidad), 'upfront complexity' (complejidad inicial, no 'initial complexity' que suena a calco). El adverbio 'though' aqui = 'sin embargo' — hedges la afirmacion.
examples: This approach scales better, though it's more complex to set up initially.
I'd argue for microservices here, but I acknowledge the operational cost is real. → hedge tecnico maduro

questions.prompt: Empieza un system design interview: 'Design Twitter's feed'. Tienes 45 minutos.
questions.question: In a system design interview, which opener is most professional?
options: Let me start by gathering requirements before jumping into the architecture.
questions.explanation: Gathering requirements PRIMERO es el signo #1 del ingeniero senior en system design. Saltarse este paso y ponerse a dibujar cajas de microservicios = red flag automatica para candidatos senior. La secuencia canonica: (1) functional requirements, (2) non-functional (scale, latency), (3) capacity estimates, (4) API design, (5) high-level architecture, (6) deep dive. Colocacion clave: 'jump into the architecture' (saltar al diseno) — phrasal verb frecuente.
examples: Before I sketch anything, let me clarify the functional requirements. What use cases matter most? → orden correcto
Let me start with capacity estimates — how many users are we targeting, and what's the read/write ratio? → mindset arquitecto

questions.statement: 'That's an interesting question, let me think about it out loud' is a professional stalling phrase in tech interviews.
questions.explanation: VERDADERO. Compra 3-5 segundos sin sonar torpe, y funciona como transicion natural al 'think aloud' — la tecnica esencial en tech interviews. Uso extendido entre senior candidates. OJO al registro: 'interesting' aqui NO es sarcasmo (como podria serlo en UK entre colegas), es reconocimiento neutro. Alternativas nativas: 'Great question — let me unpack that', 'Good question, let me chew on it for a sec' (mas casual). Evitar abusar de 'interesting' en cada respuesta — suena a muletilla.
examples: That's an interesting question — let me think about it out loud so you can follow.
Great question. Let me think through this piece by piece before I commit. → alternativa

questions.target: So the trade-off here is between consistency and availability — given the use case, I'd lean toward eventual consistency for the write path.
questions.explanation: System design de nivel senior/staff: nombra la dicotomia (CAP theorem: consistency vs availability), justifica con contexto (given the use case), y toma postura suavizada (I'd lean toward). 'Eventual consistency' es termino tecnico especifico (no confundir con 'strong consistency'). Ritmo natural: pausa marcada en el guion, tono descendente en 'availability', pausa reflexiva antes de la decision. Contraccion 'I'd' obligatoria. Registro senior: siempre justifica la eleccion con 'given X, I'd Y'.
examples: The trade-off is latency versus accuracy — given the real-time requirement, I'd optimize for latency first.
Given the read-heavy nature of the workload, I'd lean toward a CDN-cached solution over dynamic serving.
